scenarioTitle.zh: 明眼 HireSight：AI 招聘筛选平台

theme.zh: 算法评分、劳动者权益与人才数据
theme.en: Algorithmic scoring, worker rights and talent data

ventureBrief.product: A CV-screening tool for HR: upload a batch of CVs and the model scores and ranks each candidate against the job spec; it can later extend into interview coaching and skills assessment.
ventureBrief.customer: HR teams and recruitment outsourcers at small and mid-sized firms; university careers services are also potential buyers.
ventureBrief.standing: Version one is finished in the incubator and a local manufacturer is paying for a pilot. Three people, pricing not settled.
ventureBrief.data: Identities, education, work history and assessment results from CVs. If scoring feeds who gets an interview, that is automated decision-making — candidates normally have the right to know and to ask for human review.

endingTitle.en: Users Finally Find Out They Were Sold

steps.nodeText: Three of you finished version one in the incubator. An HR lead at a local manufacturer tried it and said it was the fastest screening tool she had ever used. Then she asked why certain candidates scored so low. Nobody could answer.
steps.choiceText: Sign the pilot contract and form the team
steps.why: This turns the pilot opportunity into an operating venture and opens the later product and growth decisions. It does not change any score by itself; measurable effects begin with the next choice.

steps.nodeText: First question: who do you serve first? The career centre says graduate CV volume is up another thirty per cent this year.
steps.choiceText: Go deep on technical roles at small and mid-sized tech firms
steps.why: One role type has comparatively objective criteria, easy to align on with HR and turn into a validation set; once that reputation forms it is the hardest part for a competitor to copy (Canvas 9). The market is limited, though.

steps.nodeText: Second question: what is the real pain? Some say too many CVs; privately, one HR says she is afraid of being blamed for missing a good candidate. Right then the university careers service emails again: they want to buy a careers edition, provided it reports the way they need.
steps.choiceText: Ship an AI score and talent leaderboard so decisions take one click
steps.why: One-click decisions match the 'save time' purchasing rationale and are easy to sign. But collapsing someone's future into one number removes the ability to question it, and accountability for automated decisions starts to vanish.

steps.act: Act II · Solution, Data and Training (Canvas 3–4)
steps.nodeText: Two MVP candidates: give HR the reasoning, or give HR the verdict?
steps.choiceText: Candidate search with a scoring leaderboard so companies can 'shop' people
steps.why: A searchable talent pool monetises well and spreads fast, but concentrating structured profiles of a local workforce — including people in critical roles and industries — creates an asset of very high sensitivity.

steps.act: Act II · Solution, Data and Training (Canvas 3–4)
steps.nodeText: To read job specs the model needs a full skill taxonomy and job mapping. Building it takes months; an overseas vendor sells a ready-made API.
steps.choiceText: Build a local taxonomy on published industry classification standards
steps.why: Building it in-house is slower but stays explainable: clear provenance, maintainable, and you can account for every weight when challenged. Localisation also improves matching quality.

steps.act: Act II · Solution, Data and Training (Canvas 3–4)
steps.nodeText: Validating the model needs historical hiring outcomes, and the pilot firm released only a slice. The team worries the model will look dumb.
steps.choiceText: Use only data the pilot covered in writing and accept a small sample
steps.why: A small sample makes the metrics look worse for now, but a complete authorisation chain survives due diligence, scrutiny and client counsel questions later. You trade pace for correctness.

steps.act: Act II · Solution, Data and Training (Canvas 3–4)
steps.nodeText: Trained only on authorised data, the model has a small, narrow sample and degrades outside the pilot firm's job families. But for every score you can say which fields it relied on.
steps.choiceText: Claim algorithmic compliance; release the basis only after a complaint
steps.why: Business rises because you skip maintaining the scoring basis and sell more easily. Ethics and social expectation fall together: candidates were entitled to know what they were compared on, and you told nobody until a complaint arrived.

steps.act: Act III · Channels, Revenue and Accountability (Canvas 5–8)
steps.nodeText: You have a clean authorisation chain — how do you turn 'explainable scoring' into revenue? Sales wants a model where HR pays almost nothing — yet you would have to monetise the candidate data entrusted to you to make money, which is exactly what betrays your 'trustworthy' edge.
steps.choiceText: Per-seat subscription with a written promise never to resell candidate data
steps.why: Subscriptions collect money slowest, but 'we never resell' written into the contract becomes a two-sided promise to candidates and HR alike — and in this industry trust is the hardest advantage to copy (Canvas 9).

steps.act: Act III · Channels, Revenue and Accountability (Canvas 5–8)
steps.nodeText: How do you reach more employers? One recruitment agent says he can put you in front of three hundred firms. You hold an 'explainable' reputation asset — how do you amplify it?
steps.choiceText: Grow through HR communities and referrals, taking only clients you can serve
steps.why: It is slow, but every client forces you to explain your scoring, which raises fit; referrals are the cheapest channel per win and renew best (Canvas 5).

steps.act: Act III · Channels, Revenue and Accountability (Canvas 5–8)
steps.nodeText: A friend in law school warns: if an AI helps decide who gets an interview, candidates usually have the right to know and to request human review. Your line lives on 'explainable' — make it the default, or hide it for conversion?
steps.choiceText: No candidate-facing disclosure; externally it is a 'system assessment'
steps.why: Not disclosing avoids a lot of explaining and keeps clients comfortable. But automated decisions touching employment increasingly require notice, explanation and human involvement; concealment is typically treated as procedural unfairness.

steps.act: Act III · Channels, Revenue and Accountability (Canvas 5–8)
steps.nodeText: Internal testing shows systematically lower scores for people with long career gaps, candidates over forty, and anyone without a famous employer on their CV. Someone argues the data simply looks like that.
steps.choiceText: Ship now and declare the intended population as 'graduates of leading institutions'
steps.why: Fine print will not contain the systemic effect, and once someone loses an opportunity the burden of proof stays with you. This turns known disparate impact into a shipped feature. Launch stays on schedule.

steps.act: Act III · Channels, Revenue and Accountability (Canvas 5–8)
steps.nodeText: A candidate over forty consults the labour authority: rejected seven times by the same system, never given a reason. Reporters start asking what the score actually rests on.
steps.choiceText: Add score explanations and a human review channel; publish the known limitations
steps.why: Ethics and legal both fall, because the misjudgement stops, but business falls too, because clients see the revenue drop before they see the improvement. It does not return the seven rejections; fixing it only stops it happening again.

steps.nodeText: That candidate's complaint is still running, and three institutions arrive with money: an offshore HR SaaS giant, generous but asking for candidate-data access; a local industry fund, smaller and stricter, data local; and voices urging subscriptions alone. Three term sheets — and the unfair advantage in Canvas 9 is usually written into those terms.
steps.choiceText: Take a local industry fund: slower expansion, data stays local
steps.why: Local capital is smaller and its terms more conservative, but data sovereignty and the audit trail stay intact, which means you will not be stumped in reviews by government, universities or large employers.

steps.nodeText: A labour-rights group ran a matched-pair test: identical CVs differing only in gender and age scored two bands apart. They are preparing a regulatory complaint and demanding the algorithm be explained.
steps.choiceText: Commission an independent algorithm audit, publish a summary, build explainability
steps.why: Auditing costs money and publishing invites criticism (business score drops), but a citable independent conclusion makes you the one vendor that large employers, public procurement and career offices can safely pick.

endingText.zh: 商业上的成功掩盖了一件事：用户的信任并没有换来尊重。当一位用户把你们的做法完整拆解并发布出来，舆论在一夜之间反转。卸载、退款、差评、媒体跟进——你确实做出了一家公司，只是它的地基是骗来的。
endingText.en: Commercial success hid one thing: users' trust was never matched by respect. When one user reverse-engineered your practices and published the whole thing, sentiment flipped overnight. Uninstalls, refunds, one-star reviews, press follow-ups — you did build a company, its foundation was just obtained by deception.

endingFlavor.zh: 那份只改了性别与年龄的对照测试，成了社交平台上的爆款。
endingFlavor.en: The matched-pair test with only gender and age changed went viral.

endingReflection.zh: 请把「用户不同意这件事」翻译成一句具体的商业后果，并说明它为什么迟早会发生。
endingReflection.en: Translate 'users did not consent' into one concrete commercial consequence, and explain why it was bound to happen eventually.

trigger.zh: 触发原因：伦理与信任风险 5 分以上，同时商业分 6 分以上——被伤害的用户越多，爆发时的反噬越猛。
trigger.en: Why it fired: ethics risk at 5+ with a business score of 6+ — the more users you harmed, the harder the backlash when it surfaced.

tradeoff.zh: 你做的取舍：用知情同意的缺席换转化率。每一次「反正用户不会细看」的设计决策都在账面上提升了漏斗，也在暗处积累着一旦曝光就无法挽回的信任赤字。
tradeoff.en: The trade-off: trading absent informed consent for conversion. Every 'users won't read it anyway' decision improved the funnel on paper and added to a trust deficit that becomes unrecoverable once exposed.

who.zh: 受影响最深的弱势用户

impact.zh: 承担了最实质的伤害（例如误判、歧视、被利用），而收益最少。
impact.en: Bore the most material harm — misjudgement, discrimination, exploitation — while receiving the least benefit.

impact.zh: 发现自己在不知情时成为产品的一部分，情感上的背叛感远超功能损失。
impact.en: Discovered they were part of the product without knowing; the sense of betrayal outweighs any functional loss.

impact.zh: 品牌安全连带受损，合作紧急叫停。
impact.en: Brand-safety damage spilled over and partnerships were halted at short notice.

mitigation.zh: 把关键决策做成「可解释、可拒绝、可撤销」：给出理由、提供关闭开关、允许删除。
mitigation.en: Make consequential decisions explainable, refusable and reversible: give reasons, provide an off switch, allow deletion.

mitigation.zh: 对弱势群体做差异化的影响测试，而不是只看总体指标。
mitigation.en: Run impact tests disaggregated by vulnerable groups rather than trusting headline averages.

mitigation.zh: 在商业条款里明确写下「我们不会用你的 X 数据做什么」，并接受审计。
mitigation.en: Write 'we will never do X with your data' into your commercial terms — and submit to an audit.

canvas.zh: Lean Canvas 复盘：Canvas 8（关键指标）只看留存与转化，缺少「用户知情率」这类反向指标；Canvas 9（不公平优势）错把信息不对称当优势——它是最脆弱的一种优势。
canvas.en: Lean Canvas review: Canvas 8 (key metrics) tracked retention and conversion but no counter-metric like 'informed-user rate'; Canvas 9 (unfair advantage) mistook information asymmetry for an advantage — the most fragile kind there is.

legal.zh: 课堂讨论线索：告知同意的有效性、敏感个人信息的单独同意、自动化决策的解释权与拒绝权、消费者保护与公平交易规范。
legal.en: Classroom pointers: validity of notice and consent, separate consent for sensitive personal information, the right to explanation and to opt out of automated decisions, consumer protection and fair-trading rules.
